With stable climate and growing populations, agriculture became the foundation of power — and for the first time, kingdoms rose.

On the Demon Continent, the first demon-ruled city-states appeared, built around volcanic soil that proved surprisingly fertile once the glassing residue was tilled under. On Erisdar and the surrounding regions, human and elven settlements grew into organized kingdoms with defined borders, irrigation systems, and ruling dynasties. On Tabontabar, the eastern humans began their long development toward the imperial cultures that would one day define their continent. And on Kutten, the first great elven kingdom began its rise — Elvengar, whose golden era would come much later.

These were not empires in the later sense. They were city-states and small kingdoms — fragile, experimental, learning to govern through trial and catastrophic error. Writing was invented — or reinvented — in separate corners of the world: demonic runes, elven script, human cuneiform, Tabontabar logographs. Each species believed they had discovered it first.

The pattern of Ge'orian history was set in this age: species developing separately, building civilizations in isolation, unaware of — or indifferent to — each other's existence. The demons built their first kingdoms in the west. The elves tended their forests. The humans spread along the coasts. The dwarves dug deeper into the mountains.

They would meet again. When they did, it would change everything — because above them, older powers were already stirring. The dragons were waking.
